reference.source: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Hemangiomas and Malformations
clinicalPearls: Fully formed at birth and does not undergo postnatal proliferation, unlike infantile haemangioma.
GLUT1-negative, which reliably separates it from infantile haemangioma.
Three subtypes are recognised: rapidly involuting (RICH), non-involuting (NICH) and partially involuting (PICH).
Somatic activating mutations in GNAQ and GNA11 are characteristic.
RICH often regresses within the first year, sometimes leaving atrophic skin or anetoderma; NICH persists and grows proportionately with the child.
Typical appearance is a violaceous plaque or exophytic mass with a peripheral pallor halo, coarse telangiectasia and a central depression or ulcer.
Large RICH may cause a transient, self-limited thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy, milder than the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon.
Frequently detected on antenatal ultrasound as a fast-flow mass.
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital haemangiomas are benign vascular tumours that proliferate in utero and are fully grown at delivery. They are GLUT1-negative and harbour somatic mosaic activating mutations in GNAQ or GNA11, affecting Galpha subunits that drive downstream MAPK and related proliferative signalling within endothelial cells. Histologically they show lobules of capillaries surrounded by fibrous tissue with abnormal draining channels and, in involuting forms, progressive lobular loss and fibrosis. Subtype behaviour (RICH, NICH, PICH) reflects the degree of postnatal regression.
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal and postnatal Doppler ultrasound demonstrating a fast-flow mass
MRI to define deep extent and flow characteristics
Full blood count and coagulation screen in the neonatal period
redFlags: High-output cardiac failure from large shunting lesions
Diagnostic uncertainty with more aggressive tumours such as fibrosarcoma or kaposiform haemangioendothelioma
reference.prognosis: RICH commonly involutes within months, though residual atrophy or redundant skin may require correction. NICH persists indefinitely and may need excision or embolisation, but malignant transformation does not occur.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the lesion as infantile haemangioma and expecting the same natural history or beta-blocker response.
Overlooking transient neonatal coagulopathy in a large RICH.
Assuming that all congenital lesions will involute, when NICH will not.
Failing to consider malignancy in an atypical, rapidly growing neonatal mass.
references: Peer-reviewed reviews of congenital haemangioma subtypes and genetics
management: Observation with serial clinical review and photography is appropriate for rapidly involuting (RICH) lesions, which regress spontaneously over the first months of life
In the neonatal period monitor for transient consumptive coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia and for high-output cardiac failure from a large fast-flow lesion, treating supportively
Manage ulceration and bleeding with wound care and local haemostatic measures
Consider surgical excision for symptomatic non-involuting (NICH) lesions, residual atrophic or redundant skin after RICH, or functional and cosmetic concern
Consider embolisation for large or high-flow lesions causing haemodynamic compromise or as an adjunct to surgery
Reassure that these are benign GLUT1-negative tumours that do not undergo malignant transformation, and refer complex or diagnostically uncertain cases to a vascular anomalies service
